author: r0ny123
body:
A small one. `MemoryStorage.getUniqueBlocks` blew up with `KeyError` whenever the store held any samples besides the ones you asked about: it collected the blocks of every stored function, then counted them against the requested samples only, and looked up samples that weren't in the request.

It now reads the blocks of the requested samples only, which is what `MongoDbStorage` does, and both backends give the same answer. That matters mostly for tests and throwaway memory-mode servers, which is exactly where people hit it: with more than one sample stored, asking for the unique blocks of any subset failed.

The new test stores two near-duplicate samples, asks for the unique blocks of one, and runs the same expectations against `MongoDbStorage` on the same data. Unit and mongo suites, `ruff` and `ty` are green.

author: mizzang0305-oss
body:
## 0) Intent
Prepare the MyBiz Production RLS and Auth identity compatibility fix for an explicit Owner-approved rollout. This PR remains Draft. It does not apply SQL or deploy code to Production.

## 1) Summary (Problem → Solution → Outcome)
- Problem: 15 Production public tables still have RLS disabled and broad anon/authenticated CRUD. The old authenticated `create_store_with_owner` RPC accepts a caller-selected paid plan. Existing Auth IDs can differ from business profile IDs.
- Solution: Move public/merchant operations to scoped server paths, resolve merchant access with the verified user JWT and existing binding helper, revoke the old provisioning RPC in a reviewed draft, and add a payment-verified service-only provisioning draft.
- Outcome: Exact candidate `6608c19982e5854a2d6bdcb578f3a5bcc91fa1c0` passed ephemeral Supabase CI [run 36250075155](https://github.com/mizzang0305-oss/mybizLab/actions/runs/36250075155). The Production security gate is still open until separate approved SQL and deployment operations pass live smoke.

## 2) Changes
- [x] Bug fix
- [x] Refactor / cleanup
- [ ] Performance improvement
- [x] Security hardening
- [x] DX / tooling

- Live merchant orders and order events use Bearer-authenticated, store-scoped server APIs; public store/menu/table/order/inquiry paths use server handlers.
- Onboarding setup requests use the server boundary. Paid activation preserves the paid state and resumes after login without starting another checkout.
- Provisioning checks Auth identity, email, PortOne paid status, amount, currency, plan, and request binding before calling the service-only RPC. The SQL draft adds atomic request/payment replay protection and revokes legacy caller-selected-plan RPC execution.
- The 15-table draft enables RLS and replaces broad anon/authenticated CRUD with table-specific grants and membership policies. A verified binding can resolve a business profile different from the Auth ID; real JWT/Data API tests verify own priority-settings read/update, cross-store denial, and denial after binding revocation.
- The Production-like synthetic fixture and GitHub Actions workflow test real Supabase Auth, PostgREST, Postgres roles, handlers, persistence, exact-row cleanup, and write lockdown without a remote project link.

## 3) Files Changed
- `api/stores/provision.ts`, `src/server/supabaseUserContext.ts`, `src/server/merchantApi.ts`, `src/server/adminAuth.ts`: verified provisioning and merchant authorization boundaries.
- `src/modules/onboarding/page.tsx`, `src/shared/lib/onboardingFlow.ts`, `src/shared/lib/services/mvpService.ts`: paid activation recovery and canonical provisioning reads.
- `supabase/migration_drafts/20260926_mybiz_public_rls_compat.sql`: 15-table RLS and least privilege draft. SHA-256 `dfbf994f1b52b6a6b48fe0b1b20ca50f017ec4da7c6d37c15b4110687eb47741`.
- `supabase/migration_drafts/20260926_mybiz_server_provisioning_boundary.sql`: service-only provisioning draft. SHA-256 `1f02f604e32459fbc8224fb2ec9d02d14dffaaaed9eafa5ec5b405a3bdf125cd`.
- `supabase/migration_drafts/20260926_mybiz_public_rls_write_lockdown.sql`: data-preserving emergency write stop. SHA-256 `05356a4261df67bb557ce21014480ff4f10eb6cb87d3b84d8eab244fe42990c0`.
- `.github/workflows/mybiz-rls-compat-certification.yml`, `supabase/tests/`, `src/tests/`: disposable security and public/merchant E2E evidence.
- `docs/mybiz-rls-compat-gate-2026-09-26.md`, `docs/mybiz-rls-runtime-access-matrix-2026-09-26.md`, `docs/mybiz-rls-security-execution-plan-2026-09-26.md`: access matrix, September parity limits, Owner decision, and release order.

## 4) Testing
- CI [36250075155](https://github.com/mizzang0305-oss/mybizLab/actions/runs/36250075155), exact HEAD above: pinned Supabase CLI 2.117.0 on disposable Ubuntu/Docker; both drafts apply; pgTAP role and cross-store assertions pass; anon Data API orders GET/POST/PATCH/DELETE each return 401; 903 app tests pass, 4 skip; four real handler/DB E2E tests pass; write lockdown blocks new service-role order inserts and preserves existing row; runner destroys stack.
- CI ran `npm run lint`, `npm run typecheck`, `npm run build`, and `npm test -- --reporter=dot` successfully. Local typecheck, lint, and full tests passed; built client bundle had zero files matching service-role markers.
- Production catalog read-only recheck: all 15 targets remain RLS-disabled and have anon/authenticated full CRUD. Two owner profiles exist; one has direct Auth/active binding, one has no verified mapping. Owner explicitly approved access denial for the unused unbound profile in this release. No binding was written.
- Full browser merchant screens and live Production smoke were not run in this PR. No real PortOne payment or external OAuth call was made.

## 5) Risk Assessment
**High**, because the rollout changes DB grants, RLS, a SECURITY DEFINER provisioning path, and Auth-dependent merchant access. September Production migration sources are not all present in the repository; the CI fixture covers critical identity behavior, not the complete live schema. Recheck the live catalog and exact hashes immediately before an approved operation. Pause new provisioning during the SQL/code compatibility window. The accepted unbound owner profile will remain unable to log in.

## 6) Rollback Plan
- Application rollback: pause provisioning, then restore the previous approved deployment only after confirming it cannot call the revoked legacy paid-plan RPC. Other server paths need a live smoke before reopening traffic.
- DB safe lockdown: apply the exact reviewed write-lockdown draft only under separate approval; it stops new writes and preserves existing rows. It passed on disposable Supabase.
- Do not automatically restore `GRANT ALL TO anon`, disable RLS, drop the new tables, or delete customer data. Any security-degrading compatibility exception requires a separate Owner decision.

## 7) Deployment Notes
- Target only `Mybiz Project`, project ref `plnuyudyogbzwpmdulnw`, after explicit Owner approval. No Production DB write or deploy happened in this PR.
- Server-only configuration: existing `SUPABASE_URL`, `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY`, and PortOne server verification variables. No values are included here and no new Production secrets are introduced.
- Migrations: the two exact SQL drafts and hashes above remain review drafts. Recheck September migration ledger and catalog, pause provisioning, apply reviewed SQL, verify grants/policies/RPC execution, deploy exact code SHA, smoke public and merchant flows, check Advisor, then decide whether the live security gate closes.
- Biz2Lab PR #130 and AgentOps stay on hold until the MyBiz Production security gate is closed.

## 8) Follow-ups (Optional)
- The unused unbound owner requires no binding for this release. If it becomes active, verify the exact Auth/business-profile UUID pair out of band and seek separate approval for one binding; never infer it from email.
- Separately approved Production migration, code promotion, and synthetic smoke/cleanup remain to be performed. Keep this PR Draft until those approvals and the final production plan are reviewed.

author: lloydrichards
body:
**Goal**

Snapshots and live images encoded as one JSON document, so a decoder held the whole input before refusing any of it. They now encode as lines, each checked as it ends, and consumers stop repeating codec work.

**Scope**

- In: NDJSON framing and a strict line reader, one budget meter for encode and decode, streaming entry points, validate-once in `CheckpointStore`, `snapshotEntries` under `TreeTransfer.fromSnapshot`, docs.
- Out: delta streaming, live delta commits, `Content.Ref`, binary framing.

**Description**

- A snapshot is a header line `{"format":"effect-vfs","version":1}`, then one line per node in inode order. A live image's first line holds its runtime block.
- The reader splits bytes and copies a line that spans chunks into one doubling buffer, at most twice its bound however finely chunked. It decodes each line with a fatal UTF-8 decoder. A missing final newline, CR, empty line, BOM or bad UTF-8 fails `InvalidEncoding`. `Stream.decodeText` is not fatal and `Stream.splitLines` is unbounded.
- `DecodeLimits` gains an optional `maxLineBytes`, defaulting to `maxEncodedBytes`. The reader refuses hostile input before holding more than one line, at the byte where a line crosses its own bound or the input's, so the field named does not depend on chunking.
- Given limits, the encoder fails wherever the decoder would and names the same field, so `CheckpointStore.save` decodes nothing. Encoder chunks hold at most 128 lines and 64 KiB:

  ```ts
  const bytes = yield* Vfs.encodeSnapshot(snapshot, limits)
  const snap = yield* Stream.run(chunks, Vfs.decodeSnapshotSink(limits))
  ```

- `snapshotEntries(snapshot, root)` streams fixture entries from the value and resolves `root` as the restored volume would. `TreeTransfer.fromSnapshot` restores nothing and shares one budget with `fromCaller`.

**Comment**

- Breaking: stored checkpoints and live images must be regenerated. Old bytes fail `InvalidEncoding` at `text`.
- 50,000 files, base to head: decode 242 to 200 ms, encode 205 to 207 ms. Peak RSS decoding the 14.2 MB encoding drops from 315 MB to 213 MB collected and 203 MB streamed.
- Two done-when items are not met:
  - Serialisation is 3,374 lines, not under 1,200. The Merkle fold, the budget and the line reader added code.
  - Decode memory is bounded by the budgets plus one line, not by one record, since the value being built is kept.
- In `TreeTransfer.fromSnapshot`, a directory past `maxEntries` fails at the overflowing entry, not when its listing is read.
- Checks: `bun run validate` passes.

Closes #185

author: sprimault
body:
Quatre cellules : une salle non convexe, un couloir coupé en biais, la salle
que ce portail oblique dessert, et un étage superposé sans lien avec le
rez-de-chaussée. Cinq vues, et sur chacune la traversée rend la même image
que le chemin brut — sur une carte bien formée c'est un théorème, et c'est le
seul contrôle qui attrape une fenêtre trop étroite.

---

feat(conformance): validate traversal on a level built to break it

Four cells: a non-convex room, a corridor cut on the bias, the room that
oblique portal serves, and a floor stacked above the ground one with no link
to it. Five views, and on each traversal renders the same image as the raw
path — on a well-formed map that is a theorem, and it is the only check that
catches a window cut too narrow.

---

**Les trois défauts trouvés étaient dans le décor, aucun dans le moteur.** Les
faces horizontales étaient retournées ; puis l'empreinte du couloir tournait
en sens horaire quand celle de la salle tournait antihoraire, ce qui rendait
ses murs invisibles de l'intérieur et laissait, à travers le portail, un mur
oblique flottant dans du noir. Le générateur porte désormais une assertion sur
l'aire signée, qui rend l'erreur impossible à refaire.

**Un damier plus grossier sur les murs obliques a été essayé puis retiré.** Il
rendait les murs proches en larges bandes étrangères au reste du décor, et ne
supprimait pas l'aplat du fond — lequel vient de la distance, pas de
l'obliquité. Le commentaire du fichier garde la trace de l'essai pour qu'on ne
le refasse pas.

author: pyraxxz
body:
## r42 — shared financial idempotency authority

Replaces the r41 response-cache idempotency design with a durable `FinancialOperation` claim state machine as the single authority for every Idempotency-Key financial endpoint.

> **Corrected in follow-up 3** — the earlier version of this description claimed trade initiation commits the claim in-transaction and listed it as a wired `releaseOn4xx` route. Both statements were **false**. The final truth, consistent with `docs/audit/r42-shared-idempotency-authority.md` §9.4:
> - `/api/multi-currency/convert` is the **only** currently wired in-transaction `FinancialOperation` route (its `releaseOn4xx` declaration is backed by the in-tx claim transition).
> - `POST /api/trades/initiate` is **unwired** and uses conservative **RETAIN** semantics: it clears `res.locals.financialClaimRelease` immediately before its economic transaction (proven pre-economic guards may release earlier); post-transaction/post-commit failures retain the claim and same-key retries receive 409.
> - The independent route sweep found exactly **38 `idempotency()` mounts** in `routes/` (39 at review time; non-financial `POST /api/wallet/saved` was de-mounted in §9.5 of the audit doc — it is saved-address CRUD, not a money-moving route, and forcing the financial Idempotency-Key contract onto it would have broken the production client for zero safety gain), **0** production `required: false` mounts, and **1** `releaseOn4xx` declaration.

### Contract (deliberate inversions of the old design)
- **Claim-before-execute** — a unique INSERT on `(userId, endpoint, key)` is the arbiter; there is no read/write race window to interleave
- **Fail-closed** — authority unavailable → 503 `IDEMPOTENCY_UNAVAILABLE`, the handler is never invoked unprotected
- **Deterministic outcomes** — COMMITTED replays are **literally byte-identical** (the claim stores the exact serialized wire bytes in a TEXT column, key order included — not JSONB, which reorders keys) without re-execution; IN_PROGRESS duplicates → 409; materially changed payload → 409 `PAYLOAD_CONFLICT` (exact-decimal fingerprints)
- **Permanence** — committed operations never expire; settled economics can never re-execute, beyond any TTL
- **4xx** never releases on status alone: release requires an explicit durable disposition — `res.locals.financialClaimRelease` (proven pre-economics) or `releaseOn4xx` (only where wired in-transaction). **5xx RETAIN** by default (crash-after-commit poisons the key — the client retries with a new key); **RELEASE** opt-in for provably-rolled-back transactional routes

### Wired routes
- `POST /api/multi-currency/convert` — the single wired in-transaction claim commit (RELEASE + releaseOn4xx, both backed by the in-tx transition)

All other mounts (including trade initiation) are unwired and conservatively RETAIN-based: an uncertain failure leaves a stuck key/409, never a second mutation. Extending the wired in-transaction pattern to the remaining class-B/D endpoints is the tracked follow-up wave, withdrawal first.

Specialized authorities preserved untouched: offline-POS, EWA worker, finance reversal, inventory restock (durable intent lifecycle), invoice create/payment. Full A/B/C/D disposition and the follow-up history in `docs/audit/r42-shared-idempotency-authority.md` (§8–§9).

### Proofs (real PostgreSQL, both CI lanes)
- `r42-shared-idempotency-authority.pg.test.js` — P1–P13 state-machine proofs + R1–R5 post-commit-failure honesty (incl. real fiat withdrawal) + MC1–MC3 real wired conversion
- `r42-trade-initiation.pg.test.js` — T1 post-commit retain, T2 concurrent duplicates with literal serialized-bytes replay equality, T3 pre-economics release
- `idempotency.test.js` — unit matrix for the release/retain disposition
- Response-boundary audit (§9.3): all 39 handler bodies respond exclusively via the wrapped `res.json` path (the later §9.5 de-mount of `/wallet/saved` reduces the mount count to 38; the de-mounted handler was part of the audited 39) — no `res.send`/`res.end`/`sendStatus` bypass can strand a claim

CI: broad test lane + financial-durability lane (`synchronous_commit = on`) — green on every push to this branch; final SHA and counts reported per follow-up commit.

author: jfrench9
body:
Controls for a deliberate graph writer roll (the `cycle_writers` / writer-AZ opt-in from #1547).

- **Pause and drain.** On an opted-in roll, the deploy sets a self-expiring maintenance pause on new graph writes, drains in-flight writes on each tier that will cycle, and clears the pause once the writer stacks settle.
- **Refuse at admission only.** New writes are refused when they start, with `503` + `Retry-After` from the materialize, ingest-to-graph and subgraph-fork APIs. Work admitted before the pause runs to completion. The stale-graph sensor skips while paused.
- **Alarm.** A worker log metric filter and alarm on graph write failures goes to the worker alerts topic, the inbox to watch during a roll.
- **Graph client.** A short connect timeout, including on long per-request timeouts. A connection error drops the graph's cached location, so the next call follows the replaced writer.
- The busy-counter drain is extracted to `bin/tools/wait-graph-writers-idle.sh` and shared with the ASG refresh. It fails closed when the ASG can't be read.

`just test-all` passes.

author: giraffesyo
body:
## Summary

Implements milestone M6 of [docs/PLAN.md](docs/PLAN.md). Stacked on #5 → #4 → #3; I'll retarget as they merge.

- **Subscriptions.** `hopper.Subscribe(workers, Subscription{Name, Pattern, Queue, MaxAttempts, Metadata}, fn)` registers a consumer for kind `sub:<name>`; the row is upserted when a client using those workers starts. Patterns use AMQP syntax (`*` one word, `#` zero or more), matched in SQL by `hopper_topic_regex(pattern)`.
- **Publish.** `Publish`/`PublishTx` fan a message out to every matching subscription in one `INSERT … SELECT`, one job per subscription, with the topic, a database-generated message ID and the headers in each delivery's metadata (merged with the subscription's own). No match inserts nothing. Transactional publishes notify from the transaction (queues derived from the matching subscriptions); pool publishes wake local producers and go through the coalescer. `PublishOpts`: `OrderingKey`, `DedupKey`, `Headers`, `Delay`, `TTL`, `Priority`, `Await`.
- **Typed consumers.** `Message[T]{Payload, Topic, ID, Headers, OrderingKey, *JobRow}`; `Message[hopper.Raw]` for multi-type subscriptions. Acks/nacks are the job outcomes; `ReplayDiscarded(sub)` re-drives dead letters.
- **Dedup keys** become the deliveries' unique key (`msg:<key>`, scoped by kind so each subscription deduplicates on its own); a repeated publish reports `Duplicate`.
- **Ordering keys** (also on plain jobs via `InsertOpts.OrderingKey`): the claim takes only the oldest waiting job per `(queue, ordering_key)` and skips keys with a running job, through a new `(queue, ordering_key, seq)` index; a partial unique index on running keys is the backstop. Unkeyed jobs pay nothing. Ordered deliveries default to 10 attempts with backoff capped at 5 minutes, so a poison message is dead-lettered within about an hour instead of blocking its key for days.
- **Schema v2** (`002_messaging`): subscription `max_attempts`/`metadata`, the two ordering indexes, and the SQL contract: `hopper_insert(kind, args, opts)` and `hopper_publish(topic, payload, opts)`, documented in [docs/sql-contract.md](docs/sql-contract.md). Both are exercised from plain SQL in the tests, including `Await` on a delivery published from SQL.
- **Upgrade test.** `TestUpgradeUnderTraffic` migrates from the previous version to the latest while a client works jobs in every state and inserts keep arriving; it activates with this first schema change.

**Plan changes** (same PR): §4.5, §6 (schema v2), §10 (subscription rows, fan-out, dedup scoping, ordering claim, SQL contract), §12 (upgrade test), M6 marked done. CHANGELOG has the unreleased entry.

## Testing

- `make check`: lint clean; `go test -race -cover ./...` passes 3× on Postgres 17, once each on 14 and 18. Migration 002 is covered by Up/Down/Up and by the upgrade-under-traffic test.
- Concurrency tests per AGENTS.md for the changed claim path: three clients × 8 workers competing for 4 ordering keys × 15 messages — no key ever runs two deliveries at once and every key is delivered in order; a poison message blocks its key while retrying and unblocks it in order when dead-lettered. The conformance suite gained subscriptions, publish (fan-out, dedup, defaults, no-match) and the ordering claim (one per key, nothing while a key runs, retry delay keeps the key blocked).
- Pattern table: 22 pattern/topic cases against `hopper_topic_regex` (a first version mangled `#` — the `*` rule ran last and rewrote the `.*` the `#` rules had produced, and a bare `#` was unhandled; caught by that table).

### hopperbench

Claim path changed, so measured against `feat/release` with both binaries built and run alternately (the CI gate's method), five rounds of the hot scenarios plus three of the full set, best of each:

| scenario | M4 (`feat/release`) | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| throughput, 4 × 100 workers, 40k no-op | 83.0k jobs/s | 81.0k jobs/s (−2.4 %) |
| insert (`unnest`, batches of 100) | 208k jobs/s | 207k jobs/s (−0.7 %) |
| copy (batches of 5000) | 387k jobs/s | 390k jobs/s |
| pickup latency, local wake-up | p50 1.10 ms | p50 1.35 ms |

The ordering-key check adds two correlated subqueries to the claim that short-circuit on `ordering_key IS NULL`; the effect on unkeyed queues is within run-to-run noise.

author: pixee-integration-test[bot]
body:
**Pixee Scan:** [f1f7a7f4-a66f-4bc1-8cef-4eaa697464d6](https://app.pixee.ai/scans/f1f7a7f4-a66f-4bc1-8cef-4eaa697464d6?fix-finding-id=AZVdjxO-h0BHfERFoIIK)
Confidence: HIGH Fix confidence is a rating derived from an internal benchmark and includes High, Medium, and Low confidence fixes. It comprises three weighted scores reflecting the safety, effectiveness and cleanliness of Pixee's code changes within a fix. [View Details in Pixee.](https://app.pixee.ai/scans/f1f7a7f4-a66f-4bc1-8cef-4eaa697464d6?fix-finding-id=AZVdjxO-h0BHfERFoIIK)
--- ## Remediation This change fixes finding AZVdjxO-h0BHfERFoIIK. ## Details Prevent Command Injection in introduction/views.py ## Summary Command injection in `introduction/views.py` let authenticated users supply a domain value that could be interpreted by the OS shell. ## Vulnerability Description Command Injection occurs when an application builds an operating system command from untrusted input and executes it through a shell. This is dangerous because shell metacharacters can alter the intended command, chain additional commands, or redirect output. An attacker can abuse this flaw to run arbitrary commands with the privileges of the server process. ## Changes Made The `cmd_lab` view in `introduction/views.py` previously concatenated the posted `domain` value into `nslookup` and `dig` command strings and executed them with `subprocess.Popen(..., shell=True)`, which exposed the shell to attacker-controlled input. The fix added `normalize_domain_input`, which strips and normalizes the submitted value, extracts a hostname from a URL when needed, and rejects anything that does not match a strict hostname/IP regular expression. The view now returns an "Invalid domain" response for rejected input. It also changed the subprocess invocation to pass an argument list, `['nslookup', domain]` or `['dig', domain]`, and removed `shell=True`, so the domain is no longer interpreted as shell syntax. ## Guidance Adherence **Source**: Pixee Knowledge Base Applied the following guidance from the remediation instructions: - **Prevent command injection by sanitizing inputs and/or validating user input**: the fix adds `normalize_domain_input()` with a hostname/IP regex and URL parsing to reject malformed or potentially malicious domain values before they reach command construction, which is directly in line with the guidance to validate/sanitize user-controlled data. - **Do not construct the OS command from user-controlled data**: the patch changes `subprocess.Popen` to receive an argument list (`['nslookup', domain]` / `['dig', domain]`) instead of a formatted string and removes `shell=True`, eliminating shell interpolation and matching the secure approach for command execution. - **Use validation as a guard before execution**: invalid input now returns a safe error response (`"Invalid domain"`) before any subprocess call, which follows the guidance’s intent to stop malicious input early. No new library dependency was introduced; `urllib.parse.urlparse` is part of the Python standard library, so no manifest update was needed. The change is stylistically consistent with the existing Django view code and adds a small helper in the same module without introducing unrelated patterns.

author: ctgnz
body:
Closes #102.

Four commits, each one buildable on its own.

### 1. Group the modules by deliverable

```
jmsfx-parent/          shared build config, no modules
jmsfx-core/            the API
jmsfx-tools/           jmsfx-generator, jmsfx-editor
jmsfx-viewer/          jmsfx-creator, jmsfx-server
library/               jmsfx-standard, jmsfx-hallux, jmsfx-battleorder
```

`jmsfx-tools` and `jmsfx-viewer` are real poms, because their children share a release. `library/` is deliberately **not** one — the three libraries are exactly the case where a shared version is wrong, so they sit in a plain directory under the root parent.

Mechanical fallout, all from paths that assumed the old depth: the generator's four fragment-check arguments and two config files, the server's `brand.css` directory, `deploy.sh`'s `REPO_ROOT`, and `release.yml`'s artifact globs and jpackage paths. `-pl` now selects by artifactId (`-pl :jmsfx-server`) in the workflow, deploy script and docs, so those lines survive the next move.

### 2. Bring in jmsfx-battleorder

Imported as a subtree, so its commit and authorship survive — `git log c7012a0` still resolves.

The files split across two places, because that's what the structure wants: `model-battleorder.yml` joins the other models under the generator (with a new `config-battleorder.yml`), and `library/jmsfx-battleorder/` keeps the documentation.

**Not added to `<modules>`.** The model is an *overlay* — one frame amplifier, seven values — and the generator reads one complete model file rather than composing one. There's no generated code to compile, and a module with no sources would be a jar that exists to be empty. #81 is what changes that, and this extension is what it gets tried on first.

### 3. Split the parent from the aggregator

`jmsfx-parent` holds properties, pluginManagement, build and the release profile, and carries no modules — so it can be versioned on its own, and bumping it is one edit rather than five. The root pom answers only "what is in this repository".

Cross-group dependencies now resolve through `${jmsfx.core.version}` / `${jmsfx.standard.version}`, both defaulting to `${project.version}`. **That's the seam**: pinning one to a released version is what splits a lifecycle off, in one line. In-group dependencies keep `${project.version}`, which is the point of grouping them.

This also tidied something already inconsistent — five poms repeated the literal `2.0.0-SNAPSHOT` and two used `${project.version}` for the same dependency, because `versions:set` rewrites literals and leaves properties alone.

### Three things for you to weigh

**`jmsfx-core` can't actually be split off yet.** #102 calls it the obvious first lifecycle to separate, but there's no released 2.x core to pin to — `jmsfx-core:2.0.0` doesn't exist until 2.0.0 ships. So the mechanism is in place and the flip is a one-line property change *after* the release, not now. Noted in `jmsfx-parent` where the decision lives.

**`jmsfx-hallux` is now excluded from Central publishing.** #106 brought it into this reactor *after* 1.5.0 shipped, so the release profile has never run with it present — the next `-Prelease deploy` would have published it, and a Central publication cannot be withdrawn. Whether an extension library belongs there hasn't been decided, so it's off until it is. The aggregator is excluded too, since it's no longer anyone's parent.

**Four modules were renamed.** `jmsfx-standard`, `jmsfx-editor` and `jmsfx-creator` all carried the name "JMSFX Model", which made the reactor output unreadable; the generator claimed **APP-6D** — the previous edition — in a name that goes out on a published artifact. Now: `JMSFX APP-6E Library`, `JMSFX Model Editor`, `JMSFX Icon Creator`, `JMSFX Model Generator`.

### Verification

`mvn clean verify` and `mvn -Prelease clean verify` both green: 84 tests, Spotless clean, 6,258 fragments with 0 off the shape, javadoc and sources jars building for every published module.

6,830 file renames were detected as renames, so history follows the moves.

One pre-existing wart is now more visible: the release profile logs `Error fetching link: .../jmsfx-generator/target/apidocs. Ignored it.` The editor's javadoc tries to link to the generator's, and the generator has javadoc skipped. Harmless — it says "Ignored it" and the build succeeds — but worth its own issue if it bothers you.

### Not done here

`ctgnz/jmsfx-battleorder` still exists. Deleting it takes its issue history with it and can't be undone, so I've left it for you to confirm now that the import is verifiably intact.

author: rbeezley
body:
## What and why

`offline-cold-boot.spec.ts:132` failed once, in Regression run 36094739444 on `main` at 27789167d. The issue read it as the badge going from ready to not-ready without a prime. **The trace says otherwise: the badge was never ready in that test.**

**Evidence, from the downloaded `trace.zip`:**
- The first `readyBadge.or(primeButton)` wait resolved to the **not-ready** button. 40 ms later, a one-shot `primeButton.isVisible()` returned false, so the test skipped its prime branch.
  - The page had switched from its loading branch to the class list.
  - `AtShowClassListPage` renders `AtShowOfflineReadySlot` in a different place in each branch, so the switch remounts `OfflineReadyBadge`.
  - A freshly mounted badge renders nothing until its first check finishes, and the one-shot read landed in that gap.
- The new badge checked before the page's own `syncAtShowData` finished, around 288.2 s. **Nothing re-checked afterwards.**
  - `syncAtShowData` never advances the provider's `lastSyncAt`.
  - `useOfflineReadiness` re-checks only on `lastSyncAt`, focus, online or prime.
  - So it stayed "Not offline ready · Save now" until the 15 s timeout.
- Every REST call returned 200. Nothing implicates #2452, #2448 or a mid-write transient.
- **Across all Regression runs since 2026-09-24, this test has 1 failure and 28 passes.**

## Fix

- **`subscribeAtShowSyncSettled(showId, listener)`** (`atShowDataAdapter.ts`) fires once a `syncAtShowData` run for that show has settled. It fires only after **every** scope has finished writing, including when one scope fails early. `allSettled`, then rethrowing the first failure, fixes Codex round-1's P2: `Promise.all` used to settle as soon as one class scope failed, while the entries scope was still writing.
- **`useOfflineReadiness`** re-checks when that signal fires for its show, and unsubscribes on cleanup.
- **e2e:** the one-shot `isVisible` branch is gone. `expectOfflineReady(page, 75_000, primeButton)` decides inside its poll. It clicks the not-ready button only when it is visible and enabled, never during a prime, and keeps the `data-offline-missing` diagnosis. No sleeps.

## Linear

MYK9-766. This stays open until 5 consecutive Regression runs pass after merge.

## Tests

- Red first: `rechecks when the at-show page's own sync settles` (expected false to be true) and the adapter tests (`subscribeAtShowSyncSettled is not a function`). The round-2 test "on a part-way failure, waits for every started scope" was red before the `allSettled` change.
- Every test importing the adapter, plus `features/offline-readiness`: 109 tests, EXIT=0, and shuffled 6× (the change adds module-scope listener state), EXIT=0 each time.
- `pnpm typecheck`, eslint (app config), `prettier --check`, `pnpm qa:code-quality-ratchet`: all EXIT=0.
- Codex: round 1 raised one P2, fixed. Round 2 on `d606dde75`: no findings.
- The e2e change is so far verified only by typecheck and lint. The 5 Regression runs after merge are its real test.

## Not addressed

The badge still disappears for a moment when the page switches branches. It is a flicker only and makes no claim either way.

author: ohsuhyeon0119
body:
The last three things content could build without waiting on graph-rag, Kafka or the AI work. `V7` adds their tables. Content now serves **38 endpoints**.

```
GET    /projects/{id}/memos?scope=project
GET    /projects/{id}/memos?scope=file&document_id=
POST   /projects/{id}/memos
PATCH  /memos/{mid}
DELETE /memos/{mid}
GET    /projects/{id}/favorites
PUT    /projects/{id}/favorites/{fid}
DELETE /projects/{id}/favorites/{fid}
GET    /projects/{id}/workspace-state
PUT    /projects/{id}/workspace-state
```

## Memos share one table

A project memo and a file memo differ only in **what they hang off**. Body, edit time and deletion are identical, so two tables would mean two of every query. `scope` separates them and a `CHECK` keeps them from mixing — a `FILE` memo with no document, or a `PROJECT` memo with one, would either leak into the wrong listing or vanish from both.

Empty bodies are accepted because the UI creates the card and the user writes into it afterwards. There is no version check: a memo is one person writing in one box, with no structure to merge, so the last save wins. That matches what the frontend already assumes.

A file memo can only be attached to an **active** document in that project. Attaching one to a trashed document creates a memo that appears nowhere.

## Favorites are shortcuts, not copies

The row carries no title and no order — it points at the original (요구사항 §4.2).

A trashed file leaves the list but **keeps its row**, so restoring the file brings its star back instead of making the user press it again. Starring is idempotent in both directions, which is what lets the UI update optimistically and retry.

Documents only: the sidebar's folder menu has no favorite entry, so the foreign key goes to `document` and referential integrity is real.

## Workspace state is opaque to the server

It stores the layout JSON the screen produced **without interpreting it**. Interpreting it would mean a migration here every time the tab or panel model changed.

A project opened for the first time answers `{"layout": null}` rather than `404` — having nothing to restore is not an error, and a `404` would make the client treat a normal first visit as a failure. The key is (project, user), so if a project is ever shared the two users will not overwrite each other's tabs.

## Folder model settled

Episode folders stay the **only** folder a user can create, per `TABLE_AND_LOGIC.md` §4.1. User sections are not built, and the frontend drops those menus. That closes a mismatch that has been open since the wireframes.

## Tests

140 pass, 29 new: 12 for memos (scope separation, several per scope, ordering by edit, partial update, refusals for a missing or trashed document, cascade with the document, cross-owner), 13 for favorites and workspace state (idempotent starring, trashed hidden but restored, opaque layout round-trip, per-user keys, cascade), and the migration test pinning the memo `CHECK` and all three cascades.

author: shreyaspatel031
body: ## Summary Head `708b2b9`. Submitting a URL extracts each site once, on one warm browser: a screenshot plus one in-page element read (at most 150 visible controls, plus a compact accessibility list for the page-open check). That cache is stored per study and per site (the product and each competitor). As soon as personas and tasks exist, every agent's first action is an LLM call against that shared cache. Those calls run in parallel. No agent reads the page before its first action. When that agent's own browser is open on the same URL, it performs the cached action, then reads its own page once per later step (one JS extract and one screenshot). The trace and the live UI reuse those reads. Every study result records three clocks: - time to first value: URL submit until the first agent action is visible - per-agent time to first action, from the same submit - total study time They are logged on the study, returned on the study payload, and shown on the report. Strict Linear and Excalidraw runs at 24 agents are next, on this commit.

body:
## What

A college drive-based Monte Carlo simulator, run as a **shadow** (`cfb_drive_sim_v1`). It changes nothing the site serves.

- `src/nfl/drive_sim.py` gains a `SimConfig`. The `NFL` default is bit-identical to before: `test_port_reproduces_research_week` passes with its exact-histogram check. The `CFB` config adds:
  - division covariates (off/def FBS flags);
  - wider score-differential states;
  - 2021+ college overtime (from the 25; must go for two from OT2; two-point shootout from OT3);
  - short-decay duration kernels, for the 2023 clock rule;
  - a sparse design and a closed-form sparse pace ridge (fit memory 1.44 GB → 0.52 GB, output identical).
- `src/cfb/cfb_drives.py`: CFBD `/drives` → `cfb_historical.drives`.
  - A new `{"mode":"drives"}` fetches completed weeks not yet stored, at most 3 calls per run.
  - The same file is a one-off backfill CLI.
  - CFBD names map to ESPN ids through the committed `cfbd_team_crosswalk.json`. CFBD's home/away is flipped relative to ESPN in 21 games.
- `src/cfb/cfb_drive_sim.py`: the pregame slate → `cfb_season.game_sim_distributions` and `game_predictions_drive_sim`. These mirror the NFL tables column for column, plus a `division` column.
- `main.py` runs it behind `{"shadow_drive_sim": true}` or `CFB_DRIVE_SIM_SHADOW=1`. `deploy_cfb.sh --shadow` sets the flag and adds a Sunday 7:30 ET `cfb-weekly-drives` job.
- The research code and frozen config are in `research/football_2026_09/cfb_drive_sim/`.

## Safety
- `dry_run` computes and writes nothing, for predict and for the new `drives` mode.
- Every other mode still refuses `dry_run` (tested).
- Games that have kicked off or are final are skipped. The filter is the same as `pipeline.predict_week`.
- Writes are `game_id`-scoped `replace_game_ids` into `CREATE_NEVER` tables.
- A failure is recorded in `steps` and never costs the production predictions.

## Backtest (honest)
Frozen on 2022 only: 21 variants tried, game-level margin plus total CRPS. Walk-forward, paired bootstrap CIs by (season, week).
- **Winners:** loses to the margin ridge.
  - 2023-24: +0.021 [+0.014, +0.028]; 2025: +0.034 [+0.025, +0.044].
  - Also loses to FPI and to the market. Stacked with the ridge it only ties.
- **Margins and totals:** means lose to the ridge and to the market.
- **Margin shape:** the one gain. Exact-margin log score of the sim shape tilted to the spread, 2025:
  - vs a normal at the spread: −0.087 [−0.107, −0.069];
  - vs the league pmf: −0.090 [−0.117, −0.064];
  - CRPS vs the normal is slightly worse.
- So: experimental, and the validated output is `margin_exact`.

## Tests
- `tests/test_cfb_drive_sim.py`: 24 tests, including a research reproduction check (254/254 games bit-identical when `CFB_DRIVE_SIM_RESEARCH_DIR` is set).
- Full suite: 243 passed. The 1 failure is local only (`polars` missing for an NFL EPA test that CI installs).
- Local `predict_next` dry run for 2026 week 4, with production XGB plus the sim: 117 games, 34.5 s, 0.72 GB peak.

## Deploy order
1. `bq query --use_legacy_sql=false < scripts/gcp/football/create_cfb_drive_sim_tables.sql`
2. `CFBD_API_KEY="$(cat ~/.cfbd_key)" python src/cfb/cfb_drives.py --seasons 2021-2026 --cfbd-cache /Users/VTNX82W/Documents/personalDev/mlb/hanks_tank_ml/data/cfbd --write`. Everything is cached, so it makes 0 CFBD calls and writes 178,700 drives.
3. `bash scripts/gcp/cfb/deploy_cfb.sh --shadow`

author: onlyabrak
body:
Closes #390. Supersedes the draft #394 (stale base; the rulings recorded there are all applied here).

The node answers one client's ops in one sequence, ~37 ms each (F61), so an
op's wait is its place in that queue; the RTO timed each op as if it waited
alone (after a 5 ms sample, a 13-PUT batch had PUTs 3..13 re-sent while still
queued). Rebuilt on main (the clock fix, one head-judgement, class 2, the page
recording) with the architect's rulings on draft #394:

- ONE arming formula, queued_wait(rto, ahead) = min(rto x (1 + ahead),
  RTO_MAX), ahead = ops on the wire sent before this one: at a first send,
  and at every re-arm (min with `armed`, never later), one pass in send order.
  The send order is the one `Deadline::seq` the recording labels by -- no
  second sequence.
- ANY answer re-arms (a re-send's too): no sample, but the queue is shorter.
- Only an op sent into an EMPTY queue (`Deadline::alone`) is an RTT sample.
- (i) A QUEUED first send's answer ends the back-off without sampling
  (`Rto::answered_queued`, RFC 6298 §5.7): under load no op is alone, and
  otherwise nothing would ever end it (the draft's seed 39: a page at the 60 s
  ceiling for 38 s while answers kept arriving).
- Re-sends keep backoff(attempt); a reconnect re-sends in queue order.
- GETs too (the window still caps them): the scan test checks what rule 9
  paces (no GET SENT while in_flight >= window); the window controls are
  re-derived for position arming.

Tests: the batch after a fast sample (0 re-sends, rto < 200, the lost PUT at
last answer + rto); a re-send's answer moves the batch up one place; a slow
head is re-sent alone -- at a small clock AND the browser's epoch clock; the
head still times out at one rto; under load a queued answer ends the back-off
without sampling. Setups that answered an op sent behind another expected a
sample; they now send into an empty queue (clock_origin, recording).

THE GATE (main): the FULL page model, 160 seeds, --profile model (debug
assertions on; odd seeds at the epoch origin): 11 passed -- including seeds 1,
3, 23 and 39 that failed the draft.
Mutants (tools/mutant.sh), each killed: no-position re-arm; sample from
queued ops; re-arm only on a sample; today's arming; a queued answer does not
clear the back-off; a new GET ignoring the window.

## gate --pr / live
```
gate --pr (origin/main): controls 9; members page; npm false
  page: 128 -> 133 (+5)
gate --pr: ok
```
- The FULL page model: `CRAFTWORKS_MODEL_SEEDS=160 cargo test --profile model -p page --test model` gives **11 passed** (147.8 s): two devices at 80 seeds (89 raced seqs), harsh at 240 seeds, forced straggler at 16.
- Live probe (:7813, **300 rows**, where queues are deep): **VERDICT GREEN**. Per-write median 715 ms, max 804 ms; the Sign after a median of 4 PUTs; page clock at the end RTO 219 ms, SRTT 111.1 ms.

author: r0ny123
body:
Refs #201 — it doesn't answer the WAND/MaxScore question, it gives you the number to answer it with.

The worry in #201 was that a fixed `STORAGE_BAND_DF_CUTOFF` skips a growing share of the index as the corpus grows (vocabulary follows Heaps' law, V(n) = 1412.8 · n^0.7247 here, while postings grow with the number of functions), and that nothing would ever say so. Recall at the corpus sizes I can reach is 1.000, so there's nothing to tune WAND against yet. What was missing was a way to watch the gap open. This adds one:

```
GET /band_df_cutoff_coverage                      # the configured cutoff
GET /band_df_cutoff_coverage?band_df_cutoff=500   # or any other
McritClient.requestBandDfCutoffCoverage()
```

It's a job, not something on the query path: counting skipped postings per lookup would roughly double the index work of every band lookup. The result gives, per band and in total, the band hashes and postings, how many of each are over the cutoff and the fractions, plus `max_df`, and it repeats the over-cutoff counts and fractions at 50, 100, 200, 500 and 1000 whatever cutoff was asked about, so two reports taken months apart compare directly. On the 7,244-sample corpus:

| cutoff 200 | over the cutoff | total | share |
|---|---|---|---|
| band hashes | 83,235 | 8,538,312 | 0.97 % |
| postings | 51.8 M | 111.8 M | 46.4 % |

That split is the cutoff doing its job (stopword hashes are few and fat). The thing to watch is `postings_over_cutoff_fraction` moving between runs at the same cutoff; when it does, re-measure recall with `benchmarks/compare_quality.py` before touching the cutoff.

Each band is one `$group` over the `(band_hash, df)` index alone, a covered scan that never fetches a band document, with constant memory and no `allowDiskUse`. The same shape took 39.3 s for all 20 bands on that corpus (MongoDB 7.0). Under `STORAGE_BAND_BUCKET_SIZE` a spilled hash counts once with its bucket-0 total. A database whose df isn't trusted yet gets `available: false` and a message, rather than df-less posting lists counted as empty.

Two bucketing fixes came out of writing the counter:

- `rebuild_band_df_index` only updated an existing bucket 0, so a hash whose bucket 0 was gone while higher buckets survived kept no df anywhere — the cutoff never served it and the report couldn't count it. The rebuild now recreates bucket 0 while postings survive, as the recompute after a deletion already did.
- The recompute's upsert created bucket 0 without a `function_ids` array, and every lookup reads it, so the next match touching that hash died with `KeyError: 'function_ids'`. Both upserts create it with an empty list now, and neither creates one for a hash that has no postings left.

WAND/MaxScore isn't built: it needs posting lists sorted by function id, which the fill-order buckets aren't. `docs/TUNING.md` explains how to read the report; `tests/testBandDfCutoffCoverage.py` checks both backends give the same numbers, bucketing changes nothing, the count is index-only (no `FETCH` in the plan), and the repair cases. Unit and mongo suites, `ruff` and `ty` are green.

author: breken-ai
body:
## :bulb: Motivation and Context

A Responses API stream that is cut short, for example by `max_output_tokens`, ends on `response.incomplete` instead of `response.completed`. `_ResponsesStreamState` already reads the stop reason from any terminal event (#919), but `extract_openai_usage_from_chunk` and `extract_openai_content_from_chunk` only read `response.completed`.

As a result, these generations are captured with `$ai_stop_reason: max_output_tokens` but with no `$ai_input_tokens`/`$ai_output_tokens` and an empty `$ai_output_choices`, even though the tokens were billed and the partial output was streamed. Cost for truncated runs is missing from LLM analytics.

posthog-js's `OpenAIResponsesStreamAccumulator` takes usage and output from every terminal response. This PR does the same: usage and output are read from `response.completed`, `response.incomplete` and `response.failed`. A stream ends with exactly one of these, so nothing is counted twice.

## :green_heart: How did you test it?

- New test `test_streaming_responses_api_captures_usage_and_output_when_incomplete` streams a real `ResponseIncompleteEvent` (status `incomplete`, `incomplete_details.reason = max_output_tokens`, usage 20/16, a partial output message) through the wrapped `OpenAI` client.
  - On `main` (4a138e6) it fails: `KeyError: '$ai_input_tokens'`.
  - With the fix it passes, including the partial output text.
- `pytest posthog` 4144 passed, 16 skipped. `ruff format --check`, `ruff check`, mypy through `mypy-baseline filter` and `python -W error -c "import posthog"` are clean.

## :pencil: Checklist

- [x] I reviewed the submitted code.
- [x] I added tests to verify the changes.
- [x] I updated the docs if needed.
- [x] No breaking change or entry added to the changelog.

### If releasing new changes

- [x] Ran `sampo add` to generate a changeset file

## 🤖 Agent context

**Autonomy:** Fully autonomous

- Found and fixed by an autonomous agent (Claude Code, Claude Opus) by comparing the Python OpenAI stream state with posthog-js's Responses accumulator. The failing test was run against `main` before the fix.
- `response.failed` is included for parity with posthog-js and with the stop-reason handling. A failed response usually has no usage, and that case is already handled.

Commits here are unsigned; this repo squash-merges, so GitHub signs the merged commit.

author: ppxd
body:
## Summary

- On a confining host Codex ran no command at all. Its own sandbox is a nested bubblewrap that cannot configure its network namespace's loopback inside ours, because ours drops every capability (`bwrap: loopback: Failed RTM_NEWADDR: Operation not permitted`, pinned by #2032). It now runs `danger-full-access` there, and our confinement is the boundary instead.
- The harness declares its own sandbox fragment and the stand-down that replaces it, as `SandboxSpec.WhenRunnerConfines` (`Replace`/`With`). The stand-down is `--sandbox danger-full-access` on a fresh exec, and `-c sandbox_mode=danger-full-access` on resume, because `exec resume` rejects `--sandbox`. `CodexHarness.ConfinedSandboxMode` is pinned by a test.
- `LocalProcessRunner.WithRunnerConfinement` applies the swap only inside the `BubblewrapSandbox.Available` branch that wraps the command, so full access can never reach a launch that did not get our confinement. `spec.Args` stays the argv an unconfined host runs, so every existing argv pin and every direct spawn of `spec.Args` is unchanged. A fragment that the argv does not carry exactly once refuses the launch. The field is `WhenWritingNull` and is deep-copied by `Freeze`.
- What bounds Codex under ours:
  - Confined: the read-only workspace mount (requires #2033, which this is stacked on).
  - Standard: the minimal read-only root.
  - Both: the run's own network posture.
  - On unconfined hosts Codex keeps its own sandbox exactly as before.
- Known trade-offs, stated in the design:
  - Codex's own seccomp filter leaves the stack; ours has none.
  - A Standard Codex can now write `.git/hooks`, as a Standard Claude already can. The new E2E pins this as observed, so protecting `.git` later is a deliberate flip.
  - A host-level `/etc/codex/requirements.toml` that forbids full access would put Codex back on its broken nested sandbox.
- Full access also lets Codex's commands write its config home, which the worker reads back. Two fixes follow:
  - The session-transcript capture and the mid-run checkpointer now open that file through `AgentRunExecutor.OpenAgentWrittenFile`, which is non-blocking, no-follow and regular-files-only. A FIFO planted as the rollout used to block `open(2)` past every cancellation token and wedge the run's completion.
  - Codex's model, which its stream never names, is taken from the dispatched `--model` rather than from the agent-writable rollout. Only a model-less dispatch still reads the rollout. Pricing and reviewer independence both key on this value.
- Known residual: a model-less Codex dispatch still reads its model from the rollout, the only record of what ran. That happens when a credential has no enabled model rows, or with the operator-global key. There the agent can still name its model.

## Test plan

- [x] Unit:
  - `CodexHarnessTests`: the declared fragment and stand-down across (read-only, workspace-write) × (fresh, resume); `Args` never carries full access; `ConfinedSandboxMode` pinned.
  - `LocalProcessDurableRunnerTests`: swap in place; nothing to swap keeps the same instance; fragment not carried, not adjacent, or carried twice → refused; the durable start info carries full access exactly where `BubblewrapSandbox.Available`.
  - `NativeLaunchRegistryTests`: the stand-down binds the hash and is frozen against later list edits.
- [x] Integration: `RealHarnessExecutionTests`, running the real executor, real runner and fake-CLI argv dump, shows fresh and resume carry full access iff the runner confines. Mutation-checked: applying the swap outside the bwrap branch turns the unit test and both integration rows red on an unconfined host.
- [x] Unit suite: full run green locally.
- [ ] Sandbox lane (real bwrap, pinned Codex 0.142.2):
  - The #2032 finding test flips into `A_codex_reviewer_reads_the_diff_with_git_wherever_it_runs` (Confined + Standard): the diff reaches the model and the normalized stream, and the workspace is left clean.
  - `A_confined_reviewer_cannot_write_its_workspace` gains a Codex row that requires `Read-only file system`, so the mount is what refused.
  - New `A_standard_codex_writes_its_workspace_under_our_confinement_but_not_the_system_root`: the workspace write lands, the `/usr` write is EROFS, and `.git/hooks` writability is pinned as observed.
  - New `The_pinned_codex_accepts_the_resume_spelling_of_its_stand_down`: the real runner's resume argv reaches the rollout lookup, and a bogus-mode control proves the check discriminates.
- [x] Unit: `AgentWrittenFileTests`: a FIFO is refused at once, and a regular file is read whole.
- [x] Integration (`RealHarnessExecutionTests`):
  - A FIFO planted as the Codex rollout: the run still completes, with no transcript. Mutation-checked: a plain blocking open times the test out.
  - A rollout-named model never overrides a dispatched one.
  - The stand-down argv dump now lands in the run's workspace, so it survives a confined child's private `/tmp`.

author: thegreataxios
body:
Adds `e2e/credential-providers.test.ts`. Every provider is registered in a real `createCredentialProviderRegistry` and resolved through `createCredentialCapability` with a real `credential:<id>/use` grant, against two local `Bun.serve` origins.

- Each preset and a custom-prefix provider sends its header shape to the pinned origin.
- A `Request` input keeps its headers; a rotated secret is sent on the next request.
- The keyless sentinel and an empty secret send no credential header; the credential overwrites a header the caller set.
- A cross-origin string or `Request` is refused, and a 302 to the hostile origin is returned unfollowed. The hostile origin never sees a request.
- A secret containing CR/LF is refused without echoing it and never reaches the origin; an invalid header name is refused at provider construction.
- `extraOrigins` allows only the origins listed for the pinned origin.

Adds `test:e2e`, runs it in CI, and notes it in CONTRIBUTING and AGENTS.md. Adds `@intx/authz` 0.4.0 as a devDependency for the grant.

Closes CL-9039

author: vilin97
body:
This imports the completed formalization accompanying **Order closure, order adherence and Fatou norms** by Antonio Avilés, Mitchell A. Taylor, and Pedro Tradacete. It preserves a complete weakly Fatou lattice norm (constant 2) that admits no equivalent Fatou lattice norm, arbitrarily long solid order-adherence towers, and the Gao–Leung characterization for sigma-order-complete Banach lattices.

The source is [pedrotradacete/OrderClosures at 6189ba7134f6975e7d8e4c8c093a9869d03a769c](https://github.com/pedrotradacete/OrderClosures/tree/6189ba7134f6975e7d8e4c8c093a9869d03a769c), licensed Apache-2.0. The [completion commit](https://github.com/pedrotradacete/OrderClosures/commit/5f6833f1934ac915302189e19bf083115f655be3) is dated **2026-08-26 18:19:54 UTC**; the [public paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.06689) was submitted **2026-09-06 15:59:03 UTC**. Both are in this acquisition's eligible interval **[2026-07-26 03:14:40, 2026-09-19 03:14:40) UTC**. The later repository metadata update is not used as completion evidence. Registry, directory, history, issues, and open/merged PR checks found no duplicate.

The 37-module scope retains all 17 paper modules and 20 prerequisite modules extracted from [David Muñoz-Lahoz's Apache-2.0 BanLat at b00e59836016aa1099b8011add6b07385e66428e](https://github.com/davidmunozlahoz/banlat/tree/b00e59836016aa1099b8011add6b07385e66428e). This supplies reusable vector lattices, order-convergent nets, ideals/bands, positive operators, lattice homomorphisms, seminorms, completions, and the proof-producing `llarith` tactic. The research construction supplies Boolean/Stone and transfinite-iteration infrastructure. Unused operator, projection-band, locally-solid representation, and finite `PiLp` developments are omitted; the seminorm interface and pointwise-product instance remain.

Provenance is recorded as **AI**, with the evidence and inference disclosed in the entry module: BanLat says that language models wrote much of the implementation under human direction; OrderClosures records phase-specific agent instructions and a phase-II proof pass. No particular model or precise fraction is asserted. Credits to Jaume de Dios Pont for earlier Section 3 formalization, and Michael Elliott/Anthony Wickstead for the previously announced weak Fatou result, are retained. Codex performed this port and cleanup.

The metadata follows the Lean statements exactly. In particular, `gao_counterexample` is the order-complete `C(K)` construction with large density and a closed separable sublattice whose only order-closed extension is the whole space; it does not itself assert the negation of `GaoLeungProperty`. The iteration theorem requires an infinite cardinal, bounds the ordinal by its successor cardinal's initial ordinal, and lifts the witness one universe. The Fatou endpoint uses explicit lattice norms and sequential metric completeness.

Ported to Lean **4.34.0** and Mathlib **5ed2965256430c3649e86755f9576b54eca72435**. Changes include module/public exports, current coercion and conditional APIs, TFAE indexing, typeclass coherence for sublattices, explicit proofs where stronger transparency exposed old simplification assumptions, removal of unused hypotheses, and documentation repairs. Four recursive tactic helpers are total: quotation uses the expression's structural size as its recursion bound. Three long proofs were split into CNF, projection, positive-budget, and thinned-majorant helpers. No theorem was weakened and no check, option override, suppression, or waiver was added.

Measured optimization used `/usr/bin/time -v lake build LeanPool.OrderClosures`, deleting only this project's `.lake/build/{lib/lean,ir}/LeanPool/OrderClosures*` artifacts before each run. Same Azure VM, toolchain, pinned dependencies, default Lake concurrency, warm Mathlib oleans/configuration/file cache; no simultaneous task-specific compilation in the reported controlled pairs. Shared-host timing variation remains possible.

| | Baseline (48 modules) | Optimized (37 modules) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Clean wall-clock runs | 69.98 / 71.73 s | 38.04 / 39.10 s |
| Mean wall clock | 70.86 s | 38.57 s (45.6% lower) |
| User CPU | 201.71 / 207.89 s | 139.53 / 140.96 s |

Profiling identified ambiguous expected-type inference in completion, ideal intersections, and convergence proofs. Explicit type/function arguments removed that repeated elaboration. Blanket tactic imports were replaced with direct dependencies; the dependency graph shrank from 3231 to 2587 Lake jobs. The initial baseline source and per-file/Lean profiler logs are retained. The first optimized run was 38.60 s but is excluded from the controlled pair because the audit was finishing concurrently. No heartbeat override was retained. These timings were measured at `1708a9a31` and include the Greptile-requested 11 kernel-checked tactic examples; the preceding optimized commit measured 37.51 / 34.81 s. They precede the later goal-focus repair and two additional examples at `0e45643c`. No comparable project-clean timing of that later head is claimed; its focused module validation and CI passed.

Local validation: warning-free project build; generated indexes; Mathlib's 15 linters; style; all standard quality checks in a source-identical 37-module audit checkout, with its own compiled root and empty challenge/solution libraries; axiom audit over 798 parsed declarations; compiled-environment option/axiom/backdoor audit including private/generated declarations. Only `Classical.choice`, `propext`, and `Quot.sound` are permitted. No Python source changed. Whole-pool CI and configured Greptile/GPT reviews remain the final integration/review authority.

Greptile's initial two findings were repaired in 1708a9a31: ambient-norm reductions now reuse the general paper-norm proofs; 11 tactic examples cover equality, inequalities, scalar multiplication, all four sign forms, mixed signs, positive/negative parts, and reflexivity. The mixed-sign test exposed and drove a fix to proof transfer, including state restoration before fallback. Both review threads are resolved.

The [separate thorough agentic review](https://github.com/Vilin97/lean-pool/pull/536#issuecomment-5843212820) covers every imported file in bounded packets, all four endpoint definitions and quantifiers, the full semantic port/refactor diff, dependency closure, representative implementations, and all five repository review axes. ## What lands

1. **`mayRedial` is fail-closed.** `PeerCloseError` now carries a `kind` (`network | close | peer_changed | not_paired | custody | protocol | offer`). author: marinoscar
body:
## Summary

Phase A of epic #388. `appctl deploy` assumed nginx and certbot were host binaries. The target server runs both as containers, so the publish step could not work there. This PR makes the proxy runtime explicit (`container` or `host`) and uses the correct paths and commands for each.

## Type of Change

- [x] Bug fix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue)
- [x] New feature (non-breaking change which adds functionality)

## Related Issues

Fixes #389
Relates to #388

## Changes Made

- **Runtime model and detection.** New `ProxyRuntime` type with `resolveProxyRuntime`. The mode is decided in this order: an explicit flag, then `docker inspect` on the proxy container, then a host `nginx -v`, then the default of container.
  - `update`, `certs` and `uninstall` reuse the recorded `proxyMode`/`proxyContainer`, falling back field by field.
- **Two kinds of certificate path.** `renderVhost` now writes the paths nginx sees inside its container (`/etc/letsencrypt`, `/var/www/certbot`). `livePath` stays the host-side accessor used to stat files. The module header explains the difference so the two aren't mixed up again.
- **Certbot runs in a container in container mode.** It runs as `docker run certbot/certbot` with the two volumes mounted. It no longer passes `--config-dir`, `--work-dir` or `--logs-dir`, which were writing host paths into the renewal configs.
- **Renewal now validates and reloads the proxy.** `renewCertificate` checks the config and reloads the proxy after renewing. If the reload fails, `deploy certs --renew` exits 1.
- **Every validate and reload targets the container.** Install, update and uninstall now pass the container, so these run as `docker exec <c> nginx -t` and `docker exec <c> nginx -s reload`.
- **Check severity can depend on the setup.** Checks can declare a severity that varies with context (`severityFor`, resolved by `severityOf`):
  - `certbot-installed` is required only in host mode.
  - `proxy-config-valid` runs `nginx -t` inside the proxy container.
- **New check: `certificate-renewal-paths`.** Fails when this deployment's own renewal config contains host paths. Only warns when another app's config does, so a neighbour can't block this install.
- **New check: `certificate-served`.** Warns when the certificate on disk is newer than the one being served, which means a reload didn't happen.
- **New flags.** `--proxy-container` and `--proxy-mode` on doctor, install, update, certs and uninstall. They are listed in `NOT_IN_TUI` until the TUI's Advanced step lands in #393.

## Testing

- [x] Unit tests pass: CLI vitest, 1397 tests (66 new)
- [x] Type checks pass (`tsc --noEmit`, cli)
- [ ] E2E tests pass (if applicable)
- [ ] Manual testing completed: not yet run on a real VPS

- [x] I have commented my code, particularly in hard-to-understand areas
- [ ] I have made corresponding changes to the documentation: deferred to #394 (Phase F)
- [x] My changes generate no new warnings

## Additional Notes

No new runtime dependency. The served-certificate probe uses `node:tls` and is injectable in tests.

author: fendifrost-dot
body:
Makes `main` green again. Two unrelated pre-existing breaks, the first hiding the second because Lint runs before Typecheck.

## 1. `prefer-const` false positive → `eslint.config.js`

`previewAuthStorage.ts:38` declares `let timer` with no initializer and assigns it 18 lines later, after `finish` and `onMessage` have closed over it:

```ts
let timer: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout>;            // 38
const finish = (…) => { … clearTimeout(timer); … };  // 42 — captures timer
timer = setTimeout(() => finish(null), TIMEOUT);     // 56 — can't hoist to 38
```

A `const` declaration requires its initializer, so the obvious `let` → `const` swap is a **syntax error**, not a fix. Set `prefer-const: ["error", { ignoreReadBeforeAssign: true }]`, which targets the false-positive class itself.

Chosen over an inline `eslint-disable` comment (that file is Lovable-generated — "Do not edit it directly" — so a comment would be lost on the next regeneration) and over ignoring `src/integrations/supabase/**` (which would stop linting generated code entirely).

## 2. Dead page importing a deleted module → delete `AdminPitchLog.tsx`

`src/lib/hubApi.ts` was removed in `689780a` ("Reverted probe & hubApi"), but `src/pages/admin/AdminPitchLog.tsx` still imported `callHubFn` from it. `npm run build` never caught this — nothing imports the page, so Vite leaves it out of the bundle graph; only `tsc --noEmit` sees it.

I deleted the page, completing that revert, rather than restoring the wrapper. It's orphaned in every direction:

- No route renders it (`grep -rn "AdminPitchLog" src/` matches only itself).
- Nothing imports it.
- All three links it renders — `/admin`, `/admin/campaigns`, `/admin/pitch-composer` — point at routes that don't exist.
- All three actions it calls — `list_pitches`, `pitch_stats_summary`, `mark_pitch_response` — are **not handled by `remote-bridge-api`**.

Restoring `hubApi.ts` would only make dead code compile while still calling endpoints that aren't there, leaving a trap for the next reader.

To resume that work later:

```bash
git show 689780a^:src/lib/hubApi.ts
git show 655702a:src/pages/admin/AdminPitchLog.tsx
```

## Verification — run in CI's own order

| Step | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `npm run lint` | ✗ 1 error, 30 warnings | ✓ **0 errors**, 30 warnings (unchanged) |
| `npm run typecheck` | ✗ TS2307 | ✓ clean |
| `npm run test` | (skipped behind lint) | ✓ 33 passed |
| `npm run build` | ✓ (never saw the break) | ✓ succeeds |

I reproduced the original lint error first, then showed it resolved — not just asserted the fix. No pre-existing warning counts changed, and no test was skipped, disabled or quarantined.

author: abhayla
body:
## Motivation
#933: OD-32 keeps a PDF "for seven days after its last successful extraction" (extracted text is kept for the life of the IPO row). The purge only considered an IPO once `close_date < now - 7 days` (document-cycle.ts PURGE_CANDIDATES_SQL) and `decidePurge` measured the soft window from `close_date`. So an RHP extracted long before close stayed until close + 7 (staging NSE IPO: RHP extracted 2026-09-11, close 2026-09-21 -> kept to 2026-09-28 instead of 2026-09-18), and an IPO with NULL close_date was never purged.

## Approach
- PURGE_CANDIDATES_SQL: an independent EXISTS arm makes an IPO a candidate when any of its documents' `extracted_at` is past retention, regardless of close_date (withdrawal arm unchanged).
- `decidePurge(… lastExtractedAt)`: the soft window is anchored on the last successful extraction when there is one; the close-date clock is only the fallback when nothing ever extracted. Per-document hold (item 18 s2b), textless veto, hard cap and withdrawal arms unchanged. The log line names which clock fired.
- FILES ONLY: no row and no extracted text is deleted.

RCA: the purge anchored retention on the IPO's close date instead of each document's last successful extraction.
Class: every successfully extracted PDF in both store dirs (staging, prod), every IPO status incl. NULL close_date.
Proof: tests red first (6 of 9 failed), green after; existing purge tests 20/20; supervisor re-run after rebase 43/43 across the four purge files; builder full scraper unit tier 419 files / 5484 pass. Real-data proof after staging deploy: the staging purge log line names the extraction clock and a PDF extracted more than 7 days ago on a not-yet-closed IPO is purged (read-only log + documents read).

No detection change: failure class pdf-kept-past-retention stays unguarded; a filesystem audit of the store needs VPS access and is left as a named gap

## Test plan
See Proof. Tier A review (deletes files).

## Risk / rollback
Deletes PDF files earlier than before for IPOs extracted long before close. Extracted text and document rows are kept. Nothing re-downloads a purged PDF (OD-32, by design: EXTRACTED/EXTRACT_FAILED fetch states are held and selectPendingFilings skips "no stored file"), so a later re-extraction after an extractor-version bump on such an IPO becomes a skip with a named reason up to close+7 earlier than before; it does not crash. Revert the squash commit.

author: echennells
body:
`frost_verify_partial` passes its `__global` scalar inputs straight to `scalar_from_bytes_impl`, which takes a private array. OpenCL C doesn't convert between address spaces, so `secp256k1_frost.cl` fails to build and `frost_verify_partial_batch` returns an error on OpenCL:

```
secp256k1_frost.cl:101:28: error: passing 'const __global uchar *' to parameter of type 'const __private uchar *'
```

(AMD ROCm 7.1; Mesa rusticl reports the same). This adds `frost_scalar_from_global()`, which copies the 32 bytes into a private buffer first. It sits next to `frost_decompress_sec1()`, which already reads the points from global memory.

**Tested** on `dev` 77ff44a with an RX Vega 64 (ROCm 7.1 OpenCL), through the OpenCL backend's `frost_verify_partial_batch`. There are 144 known-answer vectors, built from the kernel's own equation (z·G = ±(D + ρ·E) + λe·(±Y)) with independent Python secp256k1 arithmetic:

- 64 valid items, 16 for each `negate_R` / `negate_key` combination: all accepted.
- 80 tampered items (z + 1, `negate_R` flipped, `negate_key` flipped, wrong Y, invalid point prefix): all rejected.

Before the change, the same batch call returned error 102 (the build failure). With the change, Mesa rusticl gets past parsing. Not tested on NVIDIA OpenCL.

I didn't find a positive test for GPU FROST verification, only `test_gpu_host_api_negative`. The vector generator and probe are available if you want them in the repo.

author: mherschberg
body:
## Problem

The team protocol for reserving a STEP or ADR number — pull, push the reserve commit at once, renumber on a rejected push, scan for a silent duplicate before every push — was written out in `runbooks/collaboration.md` §2 and §6 and again, in full, in the STEP-index legend, `prompts/README.md`'s authoring recipe and the ADR register. The copies had drifted: the legend still said "Pull `prompts/`" and "`prompts/`'s shared trunk", which a mono-repo reader does not have, and each copy carried its own duplicate-scan command.

## Change

- **The legend, the recipe and the ADR register state only the rule everyone follows** — take `max + 1` and add the row (for a STEP: on the trunk, never a `step-NNNN` branch, before you branch or write) — and send a team to `collaboration.md` §2, or §6 for ADRs. Both scan commands now live only there. The STEP wording matches the generated `AGENTS.md`'s reservation bullet.
- The legend's pointer is written from the workspace root (`Code/{{PROJECT}}-docs/runbooks/collaboration.md` §2), since the seed becomes `prompts/STEP-index.md`, outside the docs hub.
- The ADR bullet carries no trunk clause: a solo project's ADRs are written during STEP-1 on its STEP branch, and only §6's team protocol puts them on the docs hub's shared trunk. Its registry note names the scans that key on the `ADR-` prefix (§6 and `./doctor.sh check`) instead of "the duplicate-scan above".
- The planning session's batch reservation says "commit it on the shared trunk" instead of naming `prompts/`'s trunk.
- **`tests/doc-contract.sh`** resolves the section citations in these four files and requires them to exist, so a pointer to a section `collaboration.md` does not have fails the suite.
- **Release notes**: one CHANGELOG bullet; the unreleased sentence saying all three scan copies find a duplicate now says the scan lives once. UPDATING's 1.8 item for the ADR scan fix now offers the shorter bullet as the fix, and the shorter legend note as optional (the legend's own scan already works).

## Verification

- **Suite, local:** 22/22 test scripts PASS under `/bin/bash` 3.2.57 on the head commit, counted by script name (`env -u CI`). This machine has no bash 5; CI on this head is the bash 5 run.
- **Reservation walked for real**, in projects generated from this commit, following only the generated docs:
  - mono solo — reserve on the trunk, branch, check 1 passes; a planted duplicate STEP fails check 1 and a duplicate ADR fails check 2;
  - mono team — two clones racing a local bare remote of the root repo: the loser is rejected, pulls, §2's scan and check 1 both name the duplicate (in both the conflicting and the silently-merging case), renumbers, pushes clean; the same for an ADR race under §6 and check 2;
  - multi team — the same races against bare remotes of `prompts/` and the docs hub, including contributors onboarded through `setup-workspace.sh`.
  Every new pointer lands on the right heading in the generated `collaboration.md`, and `./doctor.sh check` is clean in all three projects.
- **Mutation, in a separate clone:** each new pointer changed to a missing section fails `doc-contract.sh`; with the old `CITERS` the same mutations pass, so the addition does the work. Swapping `collaboration.md`'s §6 and §7 headings fails it too.
- **Review round** found and fixed here: the legend's pointer was hub-local and did not resolve from `prompts/`; the ADR bullet's "like a STEP number" invited the STEP trunk rule for solo ADRs; the CHANGELOG bullet and commit message overclaimed what moved and what the test catches; two new citers were missing from the file-presence check.

## Noticed, not changed here

- `collaboration.md` §2's note says two appended rows land on different lines and merge without a conflict; two rows appended at the same point (the end of the table) conflict instead. The protocol still recovers through §5's keep-both plus the scan.
- §2's scan is written from the workspace root; run from inside a lone `prompts/` clone it prints an error and nothing else, and exits 0.
- `check.sh` check 5 dedups ADR ids, so two ADR files sharing one number under one registry row pass clean.
- The seed's STEP-1 substeps note points at `runbooks/collaboration.md` §3 in hub-local form, which does not resolve from `prompts/`.

author: adejare-ml
body:
## 💡 What:
Wrapped NLTK's `WordNetLemmatizer.lemmatize()` with `functools.lru_cache` and pre-compiled the regular expression for non-alpha characters using `re.compile` in `notebooks/model_training.ipynb`. Also documented the learning in `.jules/bolt.md`.

## 🎯 Why:
The NLP text cleaning process was identifying `lemmatize()` as a major performance bottleneck for large datasets (like the Enron email corpus with 447k+ rows). Because word distributions have a long tail, many common words are repeated frequently. Without caching, the system repeats expensive NLTK lookups. Without pre-compiling the regular expression, it was getting compiled for every single row.

## 📊 Impact:
Significantly reduces preprocessing time for text cleaning on large datasets by preventing redundant lookups and regex compilations.

## 🔬 Measurement:
Run the model training notebook `notebooks/model_training.ipynb` with the Enron dataset. The processing time for the `apply(clean_text)` step will be noticeably faster compared to before. You can verify this by checking the execution time of that specific cell.
